Effect of the Soil Microbiome on Wheatgrass Growth in 
Moon Regolith 
 
Plant the Moon | Fall 2024 | Professional/Undergraduate Division 
 
CCA Foxes | Team #19442 
Community College of Aurora 
Aurora, CO 
 
Brianna Von Feldt, Anastasia Smith, Laila Smith, Phillip Montero Matthews, Darrien 
Dudley, and Coach Rhonda Hattar

Introduction 
As future, long term, space travel becomes a reality and projects like Artemis develop, 
establishing a renewable food source off Earth is becoming a necessity. Travel to Mars and 
the colonization of the moon will have to be preceded by food being grown on site that will 
not have to be blasted off Earth. Currently the cost for materials going to the moon is one 
hundred thousand dollars per pound (Jones, 2022). This makes sending home grown food 
to the moon prohibitively expensive. Humanity will have to create a way to turn the lunar 
and Martian regolith into crop sustaining soil. 
Theory 
To have healthy crops there must first be healthy soil. Soil is the composition of minerals, 
dead and decomposing organic matter, and all micro and macro-organisms present as a 
substrate that was or is immediately on the surface of the earth (USDA, 2024). Capable of 
having trapped gases and water within it, soil's primary importance to plants is in offering a 
medium to uptake several key nutrients. Nitrogen is a core element for the production of 
hormones and proteins within the plant. Phosphorus is necessary for plants to carry out 
photosynthesis. Calcium is used in the general growth and the production of new root 
growth. Magnesium is a component within chlorophyll, which provides the green hue 
within plants and their leaves and is necessary for the absorption of light. Potassium helps 
in the movement of water and nutrients within the plant. Sulfur is vital for the production of 
amino acids within plants. Soil also includes various other trace elements, such as Iron or 
Zinc, which aid in the same if not similar functions such as disease resilience (NSW, 1970). 
The availability of these nutrients and their quantity within the soil help determine the 
health of the plant, with other factors such as the soil microbiome affecting the plant’s 
ability to intake beneficial minerals and nutrients. 
 
A microbiome is the community of organisms that exists in a particular environment. All of 
these are made up of microorganisms such as viruses, bacteria, archaea, and fungi 
(Banerjee, 2022). Microbes are in every corner of life and contribute to human, animal, and 
soil health (Microbiology, 2017). They can modify their environment in ways that can either 
cause harm or be beneficial. Each organism type has its own set of unique microbes. An 
example of microbiomes in human health is those living in our intestinal tract (Taylor, 
2017). These microscopic beings aid in the digestion of anything we aren’t able to digest 
ourselves. This is one of the many mutualistic relationships between microbiomes and 
their hosts. For healthy soil you must have a robust soil microbiome. After a primary or 
secondary succession event such as glacial receding or a wildfire, the regrowth of the soil 
microbiome is the first step in plant life returning to the affected area. Every ecosystem on 
Earth has its own combination of micro-organisms that make up its microbiome. “The soil 
microbiome regulates soil organic matter, decomposition and stabilization, soil nutrient 
dynamics, and rhizosphere function” (Nelson, 2022). Without a healthy microbiome, 
plants will not have the correct environment in which to grow. The microbiome is vast,

“One gram of soil can contain up to 10 billion microorganisms and consist of thousands of 
different species” (Soil, 2023). Agriculture would not exist without maintaining a healthy 
microbiome for the various food crops humans rely on. 
A possible challenge of growing consumable food on the moon or Mars lies with the lack of 
an established soil microbiome in the regolith. Regolith refers to loosened fragmented 
material that forms on the surface of a planet, moon, or even an asteroid. Regolith forms 
because of processes like weathering and volcanic activity (Encyclopaedia Britannica, 
n.d.). On Earth, the regolith would include soil, sand, and other fragmented materials. 
However, Earth’s regolith is unique because it has organic matter, microorganisms, and 
nutrients that are essential for life (Encyclopaedia Britannica, n.d.). Other planets like Mars 
have regolith that contains iron oxides, which give the planet its reddish color. Regolith on 
other planets often contains unique and toxic compounds that are harmful to crops grown 
on Earth. The Moon’s regolith, like other extraterrestrial regolith, lacks nutrients and is 
composed of crushed rock and minerals. It has no toxic salts or high levels of iron oxides, 
making lunar regolith less chemically toxic. However, having no nutrients or organic matter 
makes it challenging to use as a growing medium (de la Torre et al., 2021). These 
differences are why lunar regolith is still a key focus in agricultural experiments. To study 
plant growth, researchers and educators use regolith simulants, which mimic the physical 
and chemical structure of the Highlands of the Moon’s surface. This offers a realistic 
medium to test the viability of crops like wheatgrass under extraterrestrial conditions (de la 
Torre et al., 2021). 
Wheat is a part of the grain food group and is one of the first crops cultivated by humans. 
Grains are enriched in many vitamins and nutrients that are vital to human health. In 
general, sufficient grain consumption promotes healthy weight along with reducing the risk 
of heart disease. Common foods made from grains include rice, oats, and cereal. The 
portion of wheat we eat is called the kernel, which is the fruit of the plant. Many kernels are 
produced from a single wheat plant. While there are many wheat species, their soil needs 
are relatively the same. All wheat grows best in soil that isn’t too damp and has a 
composition of both clay and sand. The soil must drain water at a pace suitable for wheat 
growth. The microbiome cultivated by wheat combats both living and non-living factors 
such as pathogens, weather, and saturation. Microbiomes in the soil can either harm or 
assist the microbes that already exist within the wheat (Chen, 2021). For this experiment 
wheat grass was chosen as the crop based on the relative ease of growing, the speed at 
which wheat grass germinates and grows, and the idea that wheat would be a primary 
candidate for a staple crop in human travels into outer space. 
This experiment seeks to determine if the presence of microbial life within organic soil 
mixed with regolith will support greater growth in wheat than sterile soil mixed with lunar 
regolith. Ten pots have been planted with wheat grass. Two have only organic potting soil, 
two have sterilized organic potting soil, three have 50% organic potting soil mixed with 50% 
regolith, the last three have 50% sterilized organic potting soil mixed with 50% regolith. The 
hypothesis is that the wheatgrass grown in non-sterile soil will have more root mass, leaf

mass, and higher chlorophyll concentration than the wheatgrass grown in sterile soil. It is 
expected that the sterilization process will kill off the microbiome in the soil and cause 
weaker plant growth. 
Measurements and Methods 
Initial Planting and Set Up 
To sterilize, the soil and regolith were autoclaved. All pots, beakers, work surfaces and 
other equipment were sterilized with Ethanol to ensure no bacteria were introduced. Each 
pot was labeled with labeling tape with each replicate being a different color. Pots 1, 2 
(sterile soil alone), 3, 4, (non-sterile soil alone), 5, 6, 7 (50/50 sterile soil and regolith 
mixture), and 8, 9, 10 (50/50 non-sterile soil and regolith mixture). To find the volume of 
loose soil that would fit into each pot, soil was placed into a pot then transferred into a 
large beaker for measuring. The amount determined was 450 milliliters (ml) total per pot. 
For the pots with mixtures of soil and regolith, there was 225ml of loose soil and 225ml of 
regolith per pot, with a (+/-) 50ml margin of error, tapping down lightly to get the proper 
volume when taking the final measurement. The sterile soil and regolith, and non-sterile 
soil and regolith mixtures were made in batches of 700ml of each soil type. Water was 
added until the soil was damp to ensure that the soil would hold moisture for the seeds to 
germinate in. The soil combinations were then mixed by hand. Before placing the soil 
mixtures into the pot a cut wet paper towel, the size of the bottom of the pot, was placed at 
the bottom of the pot to cover drainage holes to lessen soil loss. Wet soil mixtures were 
then placed in their corresponding pots based on soil conditions at 450ml per pot then 
lightly tamped down. Wheatgrass seeds were then counted individually at 36 seeds per pot 
and placed in the pot 1/4in apart from each other in a grid pattern and roughly 1/8in deep 
into the soil. 
Plant Maintenance during Growth Period 
Plants were kept in a lab near sunny, west facing windows. Pots were checked daily to 
assess lighting conditions, soil moisture and watering as needed. Bottom watering was 
alternated with top watering to maintain saturation without overwatering. Observations 
about plant health, temperature, and environmental conditions were recorded in a shared 
journal. Members of the team documented daily maintenance and notes to track 
abnormalities or any potential trends in plant development. 
Seedling Count 
During the first seven days the pots were monitored for germination of sprouted seeds and 
to assess initial viability. A final count of germinated plants was also conducted at

harvesting. The final count of germinated plants was used to control for differences in 
germination when evaluating wet leaf mass. 
 Final Plant Height 
At the end of the growth period, the height of each plant was measured from the base of 
the stem to the tallest part of the plant. Measurements were taken using a ruler to record 
the height of the three tallest plant and the three shortest plants per pot and averaged 
across replicates in each condition to compare effects of sterile vs. non-sterile soil and the 
addition of regolith. Average height and range of replicates were calculated. 
Final Leaf Mass 
The average leaf mass per plant and range of replicates was calculated in grams. Final leaf 
mass was calculated by measuring the mass of the greenery. The wheatgrass was cut just 
above the root and placed on a scale. 
Qualitative Root Analysis 
After carefully removing the plants from their pots, the roots were rinsed under tap water. 
This was done to try to remove any excess soil trapped between the root systems. 
However, the root systems were not able to be fully cleaned of soil and paper towel. 
Control groups and experimental groups were visually compared and photographed for 
qualitative evaluation. 
Chlorophyll Concentration 
Chlorophyll pigments were extracted and measured using spectrophotometry in a protocol 
adapted from SERAS SOP on chlorophyll determination and the U.S. Environmental 
Protection Agency SOP on chlorophyll determination. Fresh wheatgrass leaves were 
harvested and 1 gram of tissue per sample was separated. These leaves were then cut into 
small pieces and ground using a mortar and pestle. Acetone was occasionally added to 
help break down leaf tissue into paste like consistency. The solution was covered and left 
to settle. The liquid portion was then carefully poured into a sterile vial. These were 
wrapped in foil to prevent the chlorophyll from degrading. 
The chlorophyll extract was centrifuged for 10 minutes to separate from any remaining 
solids. 3 ml of the supernatant was transferred via pipette into a clean cuvette for 
spectrophotometric analysis. The spectrophotometer was calibrated to measure 
absorbance at 663 nm for the wavelength of Chlorophyll and 645 nm for the wavelength of 
Chlorophyll b. Data was recorded for further calculations.

The concentration of Chlorophyll a and Chlorophyll b were determined using the 
equations: 
Chlorophyll a = (12.7) ⋅𝐴663 −(2.69) ⋅𝐴648 
Chlorophyll b = (22.9) ⋅𝐴645 −(4.68) ⋅𝐴663 
Total chlorophyll, average, and range for replicates were calculated. Results are 
expressed in milligrams of Chlorophyll per gram of sample (mg/g). 
Analysis & Results 
Final Plant Count 
 
 
Initially, in accordance with the proposed procedure, 10 pots were seeded possessing 32 
seeds each. However, when acquiring the measurements for evaluating performance, it 
was a made apparent that one of the replicates possessed an irregular number of sprouts. 
Pot number 4, one of the two non-sterile pots possessing exclusively soil as its substrate, 
had a number of sprouts totaling 61 by the end of the growth period. A number that is 
impossible with the standardized 32 that each variable was supposed to have. Due to this, 
it was concluded that pot number 4 had been double seeded and as such was omitted 
from all calculations due to being a clear outlier.

Light Differences 
Day 
Night 
 
During the course of the experiment, unexpected differences in light exposure were noted. 
The photos above show the wheatgrass growing under different lighting conditions. The 
image on the left was taken in the daytime, showing the plants in full ambient light. 
However, a portion on the left side of the setup is noticeably getting less light. These being 
samples 1 and 2, representing the sterile soil condition. This also applies to the left most 
pot present within the sterile soil regolith mix, these being pots numbered 5, 6, and 7, 
which due to variation in how they were replaced within the trays between watering have 
alternated which pots were present within the dark spot. 
The image on the right was taken at night, and it revealed an unexpected light source from 
a streetlight outside the lab window. This light source also illuminates the middle and right 
side of the grow setup in contrast to the three left most pots that experience little to no 
light during the same hours. This causing samples 3 and 4 (representative of our nonsterile 
soil condition) as well as, pots 8, 9, and 10 (representative of our nonsterile soil regolith 
mix condition) to receive more light hours.

Plant Height 
 
 
Above is a graph displaying the average overall height of the sprouts present within each 
tested variable. This number was derived through taking the heights of the three tallest 
sprouts within a condition, getting an average for the tallest plants present, then 
conducting the same calculation for the three smallest sprouts within the same condition. 
Upon having the average height for both the smallest and tallest plants within the 
condition, the average of these totals was then found and used to represent the replicate 
measured. This was repeated for each replicate with one last average being derived from 
previously calculated values based on the replicate type. 
This shows that through the variables tested, the tallest growth found was present within 
both sterilized regolith soil mix and sterilized soil, both on average being taller than 20 
centimeters (cm) in contrast to both non sterilized conditions both being only roughly 19 
cm in height on average.

Leaf mass 
 
 
Above is a graph displaying the average wet leaf mass (in grams) per seedling across all 
conditions tested. Plants grown in sterile conditions have an average wet leaf mass per 
seedling of over 0.25 grams (g). With sterile soil being an average of 0.28 grams and sterile 
soil regolith mix being an average of 0.26 grams per seedling. 
These values both being greater than the average values of the non-sterile conditions, in 
which nonsterile regolith soil mix was an average of 0.2 grams per seedling, while 
nonsterile soil was an average of 0.18 grams per seed.

Root Quality 
Non- Sterile Soil and Regolith 
 
Sterile Soil and Regolith 
 
Sterile Soil

Above are photos taken of all the replicates side by side after having been removed from 
their pots. This was after having cleaned away as much of the growing substrate as 
possible from each plant with care to not damage the roots or growth in the process. 
After having removed all substrate, the roots present within the sterilized conditions 
appeared to be smaller than the roots present within the nonsterile conditions. 
Chlorophyll Concentration 
 
 
Plants grown in sterile soil had an average of 817 milligrams (mg) of chlorophyll per gram 
(g) of plant material which is less than the amount in plants grown in non-sterile soil 
(average 929 mg/g). Plants grown in sterile soil mixed with regolith had an average of 497

milligrams (mg) of chlorophyll per gram (g) of plant material which is more than twice the 
amount in plants grown in non-sterile soil mixed with regolith (average 218 mg/g). This is 
the opposite of what was seen with pure soil. When comparing soil to soil mixed with 
regolith, there was a reduction in chlorophyll concentration with regolith regardless of 
sterility. 
Discussion & Conclusions 
The initial hypothesis was that nonsterile soil conditions would promote greater plant 
health due to the presence of beneficial microbes. The data, however, did not consistently 
support this hypothesis. For leaf weight, Chlorophyll concentrations, and average plant 
height, plants grown in sterile soil mixed with regolith showed consistently better growth 
compared to those grown in nonsterile soil mixed with regolith. For plants grown in just 
soil, there was higher leaf weight and plant height in plants grown in sterile soil compared 
to nonsterile soil. 
However, some data showed the opposite relationship. In sterile soil not mixed with 
regolith there was less chlorophyll in the plants than in plants grown in nonsterile soil. In 
addition, the root system in the nonsterile conditions appears to be bigger and more robust 
than the root system in the sterile conditions for both pure soil and soil mixed with regolith. 
While the root quality data appears to support our hypothesis that the microbiome would 
promote greater plant health, the difference in roots did not generally translate to greater 
plant growth aboveground as measured by leaf mass, height and chlorophyll 
concentration. This is surprising because it is typically assumed that greater root mass 
supports greater growth. The cause of this discrepancy may lie in the potential impact of 
harmful microbes eliminated from the soil that affect top growth. 
The findings suggest that the sterilization process may have removed microbial pathogens 
that negatively affect early plant growth, and that the microbial pathogens influence is 
greater than beneficial microbes. However, it is possible that the absence of beneficial 
microbes would become more important for plant growth later in the wheat life cycle. This 
suggests that the absence of beneficial microbes should be studied in an experiment with 
a longer growth period than 8 weeks. In addition, seed and fruit production in later life 
stages should also be measured. 
The data also showed that pots grown in regolith-soil mixtures showed poorer overall 
growth compared to plants grown in soil. These results highlight the need to amend 
regolith with soil or other nutrients to support good plant health. Future research should 
focus on optimizing the soil to regolith ratio to determine the minimum amount of soil

required to balance plant health with the limitations of soil transport to space. Perhaps soil 
quantity could also be reduced with supplemental nutrients. 
If our data can be replicated, it also suggests that using sterile soil would be best for space 
agriculture. However, DNA analysis of the microbes present in nonsterile soil compared to 
sterile soil after the growth period should be completed to demonstrate whether there are 
differences in the microbiome between the conditions tested and how that impacted the 
beneficial and harmful microorganisms present. Further experiments could then identify 
specific beneficial microbes that could be introduced to the soil-regolith mix. Such an 
approach could reduce the risk of pathogen-related growth complications while optimizing 
plant health. 
There are some limitations to this experimental design that should be addressed when 
attempting to replicate this data. Uneven light distribution across the growth setup may 
have impacted some of the observed data trends, confounding our analyses. The 
irregularity in daylight may have caused some plants to grow taller as they had to reach 
further to gain more light access. It is also possible that the plants that received more sun 
generated a higher chlorophyll count due to the increased light. Alternatively, it is also 
possible that plants exposed to night light became fatigued and degraded their ability to 
continue to create normal levels of chlorophyll. Therefore, ensuring even light conditions 
and better control of experimental variables will be key in future tests. High variability 
among replicates also highlights the need for further trials to confirm reliability of the 
results. Additionally, while root mass was qualitatively assessed, quantitative 
measurement of root biomass would provide a more accurate evaluation of root impacts.
